title: Cross Process
description: A cross process look imitates developing a film in the wrong chemistry, such as slide stock in color-negative developer, so primaries skew off their true identities. Contrast often climbs; cyan shadows, magenta or yellow skin shifts, and other chemical accidents become the palette.

sections.title: Narrative function

blocks.text: Wrong chemistry on purpose. Fashion films and music videos of the 1990s used the accident as style: skies go odd, shadows pick up cyan or green, skin slides toward magenta or jaundice.
The world looks like a lab error you kept. It is the wrong tool when you wanted true hues only louder.
That is Hyper-Saturation. It is the wrong tool for a designed complementary split with protected skin (Teal and Orange).
Vaporwave may borrow skewed primaries as a genre costume; cross-process is the chemical alibi, not the nostalgia package.

sections.title: How it works

blocks.text: Offset primary relationships: push shadows toward cyan or green, let highlights go yellow, magenta, or red depending on the stock story, and raise contrast. Skin will not grade like a commercial unless you isolate it, which fights the look.
Do not randomly assign hues shot to shot; pick one accident and keep it. Prompt: Cross-processed look on [Subject], skewed primaries, cyan shadows, magenta skin shift, music-video chemical accident.

sections.title: When to use it

blocks.text: Use it when the image should look like a kept lab error: a 1990s fashion clip, a music video, an unreliable night. Do not use it as loud-but-true color, and do not confuse it with teal-orange.

sections.title: In film

blocks.text: 1990s fashion films and music videos are the grammar: chemical accident as style, not a single canonical feature. When a narrative film borrows it, the tell is displaced primaries rather than simple loud red.
Treat those clips as the reference class.

sections.title: What usually goes wrong

blocks.text: The usual wrong cousin is Hyper-Saturation or Teal and Orange. The tell is correct reds that are only louder, or peach faces on cyan streets in a studio-split pattern.
Fix: hues that have slipped to the wrong neighbors, contrasty accident, skin not commercially protected.

sections.title: Questions

blocks.text: What is cross process in film?
It is the look of film developed in the wrong chemistry, or a digital imitation of that mismatch. Primaries skew, contrast often rises, and skin and shadows take on unnatural neighbors.
Cross Process vs Hyper-Saturation
Hyper-saturation makes true hues louder. Cross-process puts hues in the wrong place: cyan shadows, magenta skin, yellow highlights. Loud is not the same as wrong.
When should I use cross process?
Use it for a kept chemical accident: fashion, music video, unreliable color. Skip it when hues should be true, even if loud, or when you wanted a teal-orange split.
How do I prompt cross process for AI image or video?
Write: Cross-processed look on [Subject], skewed primaries, cyan shadows, magenta skin shift, music-video chemical accident. Forbid correct loud primaries and protected peach skin.
